newsitem.title: UK: Attack on police hits N.Ireland peace process.
newsitem.headline: Attack on police hits N.Ireland peace process.

text.p: A suspected IRA bomb attack on a police patrol further strained the already badly damaged Northern Irish peace process on Wednesday, prompting fears of more sectarian and political violence.

The explosion occurred in the Shantallow area of the province's second city of Londonderry on Tuesday night as a two-vehicle police patrol was passing, a police spokesman said. None of the police officers was injured.

There was no immediate claim of responsibility for the attack but security sources said it bore the hallmarks of the IRA (Irish Republican Army), which is fighting to end British rule in Northern Ireland. The spokesman said it was not immediately clear if the bomb had exploded at the side of the road or whether it had been fired at the patrol.

The attack formed part of a growing pattern of violence in Northern Ireland and sparked further fears that pro-British "Loyalist" guerrillas would end their two-year ceasefire and retaliate against the IRA.
Police in Belfast questioned two men arrested after the IRA launched a rocket attack against the city's High Court building on Monday, injuring a police officer.
That attack was followed by a series of hoax bomb warnings. IRA guerrillas apparently hoped the hoax calls would bring the city to a standstill.
Earlier on Tuesday, police carried out a controlled explosion on a suspect car in Belfast and evacuated the Europa hotel after a telephoned bomb warning. No device was found.
The IRA's political wing Sinn Fein, which has refused to condemn guerrilla violence, has stepped up its campaign for an immediate place at multi-party peace talks on Northern Ireland.
British Prime Minister John Major, an architect of the slow-moving Northern Ireland peace process, said Monday's Belfast attack made it hard to believe Sinn Fein could take part in the negotiations.
"It is certainly going to be extremely difficult to see how the IRA can persuade anyone that Sinn Fein should re-enter the talks," Major told BBC radio.
Sinn Fein has been excluded from the talks until the IRA calls a permanent halt to the bombing campaign it launched last February when it ended a 17-month truce.

Despite police fears that IRA violence could mean an end to the Protestant Loyalists' 26-month truce, spokesmen for closely allied political groups have said that as far as they knew the ceasefire was still intact.
Newspaper reports last weekend quoted Loyalist activists as saying they would avenge IRA violence with attacks of their own.
